italianate.title: Italianate (courthouse-square type)
italianate.note: A two-story brick Italianate of the 1850s-60s, like the Van Epps and Brookner houses: a near-square block with tall 12 ft stories, a low hip roof on deep bracketed eaves, a belvedere, a flat-roofed entry porch, a side bay, and a one-story rear kitchen wing.
gaps: The side bay is canted (octagonal) on the real houses; structures are rectangles, so it is a square box bay.
The rear wing's own lower story height (8-9 ft against the main block's 12 ft) cannot be set: story height is building-wide.
The entry porch's flat roof usually carries a balustrade: a railing on a roof edge, not yet a facade element.
Paired brackets, tall arched windows, and hood molds are facade modifiers (not built yet).

upright-and-wing.title: Upright-and-wing (gable-front-and-wing)
upright-and-wing.note: The most common Midwestern farmhouse and town house of 1860-1900: a two-story gable-front "upright" with a lower one-and-a-half-story side wing, and a porch in the ell along the wing.
gaps: The wing is a story and a half: a knee wall under a steep roof. Stories are whole, so it is one story with a tall roof.

queen-anne.title: Gable-front Queen Anne (Reagan Boyhood Home type)
queen-anne.note: A two-story frame Queen Anne of the 1890s like the Reagan Boyhood Home (1891): a steep gable-front main block, a two-story cross-gabled side projection, and a front porch wrapping one corner.
gaps: Towers and turrets (round or polygonal, often with a conical roof) cannot be modeled: structures are rectangles.
Gable-end detailing (fish-scale shingles, spindlework, bargeboards) is facade work.

foursquare.title: American Foursquare
foursquare.note: The standard Midwestern house of 1900-1930: a two-and-a-half-story square box, a hip roof with hipped dormers, and a full-width front porch on columns.
gaps: Porch columns on brick piers with a solid half wall between are facade/railing work; posts are plain boxes.

refused.label: hip dormer 2.4 m wide, 1.1 m walls, under a 6:12 roof
errors: The structure crosses a hip, ridge, or valley of the host roof; it must stand on one roof face.
warnings: The structure's roof was lowered to meet the host ridge.

bungalow.title: Craftsman bungalow
bungalow.note: A story-and-a-half side-gabled bungalow of the 1910s-20s: a broad low roof on deep eaves, a wide shed dormer, and a front-gabled porch on tapered piers.
gaps: Many bungalows have an integral porch: the main roof carries on over a porch recessed into the footprint. A recess at ground level would need a notch in the footprint with the roof running on over it; only dormers can be recessed.
Exposed rafter tails, knee braces, and tapered piers are facade work.

dutch-colonial.title: Dutch Colonial Revival
dutch-colonial.note: A 1910s-30s Dutch Colonial: a side-gabled gambrel whose steep lower slopes hold the second floor, a long shed dormer across the front, and a gabled entry hood.
gaps: The characteristic full-width shed dormer runs from the lower slope up past the break to meet the upper slope. A dormer must stay on one roof face, so the built one is a low band under the break.
An entry hood is a roof on brackets over the door with no floor or posts; the model has only porches, so it stands on a small stoop with posts.

refused.label: full shed dormer rising from the lower slope to meet the upper slope near the ridge
errors: The structure crosses a hip, ridge, or valley of the host roof; it must stand on one roof face.

farmhouse.title: I-house farmhouse with rear ell
farmhouse.note: A two-story, one-room-deep I-house (common across northern Illinois from the 1850s) with a two-story rear ell, a full-width front porch, and a side porch along the ell.

cape-cod.title: Cape Cod (1940s)
cape-cod.note: A 1940s story-and-a-half Cape Cod: a steep side-gabled roof with two gabled dormers and a small gabled entry.
gaps: The entry is often an enclosed vestibule or just a hood; here it is an open stoop.
Dormer spacing is set by window bays; placing dormers by the facade layout is not linked yet.

ranch.title: L-shaped ranch (1950s)
ranch.note: A 1950s one-story ranch: a long low hip roof over an L with a front-facing garage wing, and a recessed entry porch in the ell.
gaps: On a real ranch the main roof usually carries on over the entry porch; here the porch has its own shed roof tucked under the eave.
The continuous (straight-skeleton) hip has no eave overhang or fascia, so the low, deep eaves that define a ranch are missing.
A garage has a lower floor (at grade) than the house; floor levels are building-wide.
